key_insight: Wake capture during plate reversal produces excess drag beyond quasi-steady prediction, and its size/timing are governed mainly by how far the plate traveled before reversing.
engineering_relevance: For flapping and reciprocating systems, wake history can materially change force loads, so stroke design and reversal timing should account for vortex interaction, not just instantaneous kinematics.
method: Translational forward-and-back flat-plate experiment at insect-flight-relevant Reynolds numbers.
Measure drag during reversal and compare against quasi-steady estimates to isolate excess wake-induced force.
Interpret the wake using a simplified point-vortex model for the starting vortex ring.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports observed excess drag, two distinct wake-force peaks linked to vortex detachment/re-formation, and a scaling law with pre-reversal distance described by combined fourth-root and linear dependence.
watch_item: The minimal point-vortex model captures scaling qualitatively, but real flapping wakes are three-dimensional and may deviate when vortex topology or Reynolds number changes.
paper_title: Reversal of a flat plate into its wake: a minimal model for wake capture
